sm: Ben Shapiro opens by noting that everyone is excited about the long-awaited release of Grand Theft Auto 6, thirteen years after the last game. He says the marketing campaign may be the greatest in history, citing a Miami Heat court painted in the game's colors and a weather channel post tied to the game. Pre-orders are estimated to have passed one and a half billion dollars, and a PlayStation outage hit just before launch.

He describes how many fans are taking time off to play. A survey found thirty-nine percent of respondents requested leave, averaging four days, and one in five salaried workers plan to take off, including thirty-two percent of Gen Z workers. He grants that big cultural events can be charming, but argues the game is bad for society because it centers on random criminality. He previews three reasons: celebrating immorality harms a society, catering to the worst impulses of young men is self-destructive, and putting bad material before your eyes damages your soul.

Shapiro argues Americans have accepted a higher level of immorality and now celebrate it. He reads glowing reviews from The New York Times and The Guardian that praise the game's love story and small rewards for kindness, while admitting it earns its adult rating with drug use, nudity and strip clubs. He says the reviewers barely register how extreme the content is.

He then traces the series' history from 1997 through GTA 5, noting that Rockstar welcomed outrage. In the early 2000s Joe Lieberman, Sam Brownback and Hillary Clinton all condemned the games, and the House passed a bipartisan resolution in 2005 over hidden content in San Andreas. Today, he says, that cultural objection has vanished. Miami-Dade County spent four million dollars on the game, streamers play it live, Representative Maxwell Frost says it is just a game, and the White House posted a joke about it.

He concludes that ubiquity cancels out moral objections. The few remaining taboos in the game are about avoiding real-life tragedies, not about morality, and a twelve-year-old playing it would no longer surprise anyone.

Shapiro says the game is young male wish fulfillment. Pre-orders were eighty-five percent male, and surveys show most players started before eighteen and many before twelve. He ties this to politics and the push to win young men, arguing young men are driven by testosterone toward aggression and sex. Channeled well, that drive builds and defends; left unchanneled, George Gilder's naked nomads become destructive.

He blames feminism for dismissing male drive as evil and dismantling marriage, fatherhood and the roles of police and military that once channeled it. He adds that some blowback to the game comes from young men angry that prostitutes were removed. He plays clips of the main character shooting a woman and taking a selfie with the corpse, a player causing random chaos, and a plane hijacking.

He notes that the game still has limits, such as no pushing people onto subway tracks and an immortal protester character. He admits one sequence, in which protesters open a truck and a polar bear attacks, is funny and subversive. But he says building whole worlds that humor the worst impulses is bad for society, since the virtual world shapes how young people think and respond in real life.

For his third reason, Shapiro says what you put in your head shapes who you are and does spiritual damage. He says not all recreation is equal, comparing pornography to watching Casablanca, and argues the game desensitizes players to immorality. Habituation is real, so the dopamine hit of a chase fades with repetition, as with pornography. He cites Numbers, Philippians and Romans on guarding what you look at and renewing your mind.

He quotes a Rockstar executive saying the game aims to be more satirical and grotesque than a mirror of the world. As taboos are pushed out, he says, new ones must be found, until nothing is left to violate. He cites Camille Paglia saying subversion needs limits to break. He then plays Jordan Peterson describing young relatives glued to their phones, and reads a Free Press writer saying the game's world is so realistic it feels built to replace real life rather than augment it.

Shapiro jokes about a Babylon Bee parody called Grand Faith Auto, then turns to the day's economic story, the Anthropic IPO. Axios reported it raised over eighty-one billion dollars at eighty-three dollars a share, valuing the company above one trillion dollars, the largest IPO in American history. He does not think it is overvalued. Revenue rose from about four and a half billion in 2025 to over thirty billion so far in 2026. About eighty percent comes from usage by businesses and developers, and twenty percent from individual plans. He says thousands of employees became millionaires.

He praises Claude and plays Daniela Amodei describing clinicians using a medical tool powered by it. He says Anthropic is insulated from Nvidia troubles because it uses several chip makers. The main risk is a drop in demand or costlier data centers. He warns of a coming backlash against AI, including a group of former employees attacking the company, Joy Reid saying tech leaders should be deported, Democrats threatening to investigate Elon Musk, and Gavin Newsom proposing state powers to shut down risky models.

Shapiro then contrasts Europe, where Christine Lagarde admitted entrepreneurs struggle to raise money across fragmented markets, with a United States youth unemployment rate near ten percent. He mocks Zohran Mamdani's remarks at a Deal Book event. Finally he covers the president's meetings in China and with Russia on oil, nuclear arsenals and the International Criminal Court. He notes China's arsenal has grown to about six hundred warheads, that Putin denied starting the Ukraine war, and that Trump praised Xi Jinping. He calls the UN useless and welcomes Trump's dismissal of the ICC, but sees few real results.
